title: Functions
description: Function notation, domain and range, composite and inverse functions, transformations, and odd/even functions.

notes.heading: Function Notation, Domain, Range
notes.body:
A function is a rule that takes an input and produces exactly one output. Every IB question about functions starts with understanding these three ideas: notation, domain, and range.

📌 Definition
A function $f$ maps each element of the domain to exactly one element of the range.

    $$f: x \to f(x)$$

    $x$ = input (independent variable)
    $f(x)$ = output (dependent variable)

🔑 Domain and Range
    Domain  = set of all valid inputs
    Range   = set of all actual outputs

    Example: $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 2}$
        Domain:  $x - 2 \geq 0$  →  $x \geq 2$
        Range:   $\sqrt{x - 2} \geq 0$  →  $f(x) \geq 0$

💡 Worked Example 1 — Finding domain and range
Find the domain and range of $f(x) = \frac{1}{x + 3}$.

  Step 1: Identify restrictions on the domain
    The denominator cannot be zero:
    $x + 3 \neq 0$  →  $x \neq -3$

  Step 2: State the domain
    Domain: all real $x$, $x \neq -3$

  Step 3: Find the range
    As $x \to -3$, $f(x) \to \pm\infty$. As $x \to \pm\infty$, $f(x) \to 0$.
    $f(x)$ can take any real value except $0$.
    Range: all real $f(x)$, $f(x) \neq 0$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Using function notation
For $f(x) = x^3 + 1$ with domain $2 \leq x \leq 10$:

  Step 1: Evaluate $f(7)$
    $f(7) = 7^3 + 1 = 343 + 1 = 344$

  Step 2: Find the range
    $f(x)$ is increasing on $[2, 10]$
    Minimum: $f(2) = 2^3 + 1 = 9$
    Maximum: $f(10) = 10^3 + 1 = 1001$
    Range: $9 \leq f(x) \leq 1001$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The domain must always be stated; if not stated, assume all real values that work
• Use interval notation or inequalities to write domains and ranges
• The vertical line test checks if a graph represents a function
• $\mathbb{R}$ means all real numbers; common subsets are $\mathbb{Z}$ (integers), $\mathbb{Q}$ (rationals), $\mathbb{N}$ (natural numbers)

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing domain and range. The domain is about $x$-values (horizontal); the range is about $y$-values (vertical). When you see $f(x) \geq 0$, that describes the range, not the domain.

notes.heading: Composite and Inverse Functions
notes.body:
Composite functions chain two functions together. Inverse functions undo each other. Both are central to solving equations and modelling real-world problems.

📌 Composite Function Definition
    $$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$$

    Apply $g$ first, then apply $f$ to the result.
    Order matters: $(f \circ g)(x)$ is usually NOT equal to $(g \circ f)(x)$.

🔑 Domain of a Composite Function
    Domain of $f \circ g$ = { $x$ in domain of $g$  |  $g(x)$ is in domain of $f$ }

📌 Inverse Function Definition
    $f^{-1}$ reverses the mapping of $f$.

    $$f(f^{-1}(x)) = x \quad \text{and} \quad f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$$

    An inverse exists only if $f$ is one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test).

🔑 Finding the Inverse — Step by Step
    Step 1: Write $y = f(x)$
    Step 2: Swap $x$ and $y$
    Step 3: Solve for $y$
    Step 4: Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x)$

💡 Worked Example 1 — Composite function
Given $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 4}$ and $g(x) = 3 + 2x$, find $(f \circ g)(x)$.

  Step 1: Write the composition
    $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f(3 + 2x)$

  Step 2: Substitute into $f$
    $f(3 + 2x) = \sqrt{(3 + 2x) + 4} = \sqrt{2x + 7}$

  Step 3: State the domain of the composite
    Need $2x + 7 \geq 0$  →  $x \geq -\frac{7}{2}$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Finding an inverse
Find the inverse of $f(x) = 2x + 5$.

  Step 1: Let $y = 2x + 5$

  Step 2: Swap $x$ and $y$
    $x = 2y + 5$

  Step 3: Solve for $y$
    $x - 5 = 2y$
    $y = \frac{x - 5}{2}$

  Step 4: Write the inverse
    $$f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 5}{2}$$

💡 Worked Example 3 — Restricted domain and inverse
The function $f(x) = (x - 2)^2 + 5$, $x \leq m$ has an inverse.

  Step 1: Find the largest possible $m$
    The parabola has vertex at $(2, 5)$. To be one-to-one, restrict to one side of the vertex.
    Largest $m = 2$ (so $x \leq 2$)

  Step 2: Find the inverse
    $y = (x - 2)^2 + 5$
    $x = (y - 2)^2 + 5$
    $(y - 2)^2 = x - 5$
    Since $y \leq 2$ for the inverse, take the negative root:
    $y - 2 = -\sqrt{x - 5}$
    $$f^{-1}(x) = 2 - \sqrt{x - 5}$$

  Step 3: Domain of $f^{-1}$
    Range of $f$ is $f(x) \geq 5$, so domain of $f^{-1}$ is $x \geq 5$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of $f$ in the line $y = x$
• Domain of $f$ becomes range of $f^{-1}$; range of $f$ becomes domain of $f^{-1}$
• Many-to-one functions can have inverses if the domain is restricted first
• For quadratics, restrict at the vertex ($x \geq h$ or $x \leq h$)
• Self-inverse functions satisfy $f = f^{-1}$ (example: $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$)

⚠️ Common Mistake
Getting the order wrong in composite functions. $(f \circ g)(x)$ means $g$ first, then $f$ — the function closest to $x$ is applied first. Also, forgetting to restrict the range when finding the inverse of a quadratic. If the original domain was $x \leq 2$, the inverse must satisfy $f^{-1}(x) \leq 2$, so you must choose the negative square root.

notes.heading: Transformations
notes.body:
Transformations let you move, stretch, and flip graphs without redrawing from scratch. Knowing the rules saves time in exams and helps you sketch unfamiliar functions quickly.

📌 Transformation Rules
Given $y = f(x)$, each change below produces a specific geometric effect:

    $$\begin{aligned}
    y &= f(x) + a && \text{vertical translation by $a$ units (up if $a > 0$)} \\n    y &= f(x - a) && \text{horizontal translation by $a$ units (right if $a > 0$)} \\n    y &= a \cdot f(x) && \text{vertical stretch by factor $a$} \\
    y &= f(ax) && \text{horizontal stretch by factor $\frac{1}{a}$} \\n    y &= -f(x) && \text{reflection in the $x$-axis} \\n    y &= f(-x) && \text{reflection in the $y$-axis}
    \end{aligned}$$

🔑 Order Matters for Multiple Transformations
    Horizontal transformations: apply in the REVERSE order of operations
    Vertical transformations: apply in the NORMAL order of operations

💡 Worked Example 1 — Identifying transformations
Describe the transformation that maps $y = f(x)$ to $y = 3f(x) - 2$.

  Step 1: Identify the vertical stretch
    $y = 3f(x)$ is a vertical stretch by factor $3$

  Step 2: Identify the vertical translation
    $y = 3f(x) - 2$ is a translation down by $2$ units

  Step 3: State the order
    Stretch first, then translate (normal order for vertical)

💡 Worked Example 2 — Composite horizontal transformation
Describe the transformation that maps $y = f(x)$ to $y = f(2x - 1)$.

  Step 1: Factor the argument
    $y = f(2x - 1) = f(2(x - \frac{1}{2}))$

  Step 2: Identify the horizontal stretch
    $y = f(2x)$ is a horizontal stretch by factor $\frac{1}{2}$

  Step 3: Identify the horizontal translation
    $y = f(2(x - \frac{1}{2}))$ is a translation right by $\frac{1}{2}$ unit

  Step 4: State the order
    Translate right by $\frac{1}{2}$ first, then stretch horizontally by $\frac{1}{2}$
    (reverse order for horizontal transformations)

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Horizontal translations use $(x - a)$ inside the function — counter-intuitive direction
• Horizontal stretches use $f(x/q)$ — stretch factor is $q$, not $1/q$
• Reflections are special cases of stretches with negative scale factors
• Asymptotes move with translations but not with stretches in the perpendicular direction
• For $y = a \cdot f(x) + b$: stretch by $a$, then translate by $b$
• For $y = f(ax + b)$: translate by $-b$, then stretch by $\frac{1}{a}$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking $y = f(x + 3)$ shifts the graph right by $3$. It shifts LEFT by $3$. Remember: replace $x$ with $(x - a)$ for a right shift, so $(x + 3) = (x - (-3))$ means shift left $3$ units. Another common error: confusing horizontal and vertical stretch factors — $y = f(2x)$ compresses horizontally by $\frac{1}{2}$, it does NOT stretch.

notes.heading: Odd and Even Functions
notes.body:
Symmetry properties of functions simplify integration, graph sketching, and algebraic manipulation. Two important symmetry types are even and odd.

📌 Definitions
    $$\text{Even function: } f(-x) = f(x) \quad \text{for all $x$ in the domain}$$
    $$\text{Odd function: } f(-x) = -f(x) \quad \text{for all $x$ in the domain}$$

🔑 Geometric Meaning
    Even → symmetric about the $y$-axis
    Odd  → $180^\circ$ rotational symmetry about the origin

💡 Worked Example 1 — Testing for even
Show that $f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2$ is even.

  Step 1: Find $f(-x)$
    $f(-x) = (-x)^4 - 3(-x)^2$

  Step 2: Simplify
    $f(-x) = x^4 - 3x^2 = f(x)$

  Step 3: Conclude
    Since $f(-x) = f(x)$, the function is even.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Testing for odd
Show that $f(x) = x^3 - x$ is odd.

  Step 1: Find $f(-x)$
    $f(-x) = (-x)^3 - (-x) = -x^3 + x$

  Step 2: Factor out $-1$
    $f(-x) = -(x^3 - x) = -f(x)$

  Step 3: Conclude
    Since $f(-x) = -f(x)$, the function is odd.

💡 Worked Example 3 — A function that is neither
Test $f(x) = x^2 + x$ for symmetry.

  Step 1: Find $f(-x)$
    $f(-x) = (-x)^2 + (-x) = x^2 - x$

  Step 2: Compare with $f(x)$ and $-f(x)$
    $f(-x) \neq f(x)$  (not even)
    $f(-x) \neq -f(x) = -x^2 - x$  (not odd)

  Step 3: Conclude
    The function is neither even nor odd.

📎 Common Even and Odd Functions
• Even: $x^2$, $x^4$, $\cos x$, $|x|$, constants
• Odd: $x$, $x^3$, $\sin x$, $\tan x$
• Neither: most polynomials with both odd and even powers

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The sum of two even functions is even
• The sum of two odd functions is odd
• The product of two even functions is even
• The product of two odd functions is even
• The product of an even and an odd function is odd

⚠️ Common Mistake
Assuming all polynomial functions are either even or odd. Most functions are neither. Also, forgetting to test the ENTIRE function — you must substitute $-x$ into every term, not just the ones that look convenient.

notes.heading: Piecewise Functions
notes.body:
Piecewise functions use different formulas on different intervals. They model real-world situations where rules change at specific boundaries, like taxi fares or tax brackets.

📌 Definition
A piecewise function is defined by different expressions on different intervals.

    $$f(x) = \begin{cases} g(x) & \text{for $x$ in interval A} \\ h(x) & \text{for $x$ in interval B} \end{cases}$$

    The intervals must not overlap.

🔑 Evaluating a Piecewise Function
    1. Identify which interval contains the input value
    2. Use the corresponding formula
    3. The domain is the union of all intervals

💡 Worked Example 1 — Evaluating a piecewise function
For the piecewise function

    $$f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x - 5 & \text{for $-10 \leq x \leq 10$} \\ 3x + 1 & \text{for $x > 10$} \end{cases}$$

Find $f(0)$, $f(10)$, and $f(20)$.

  Step 1: Evaluate $f(0)$
    $0$ is in $[-10, 10]$, so use $f(x) = 2x - 5$
    $f(0) = 2(0) - 5 = -5$

  Step 2: Evaluate $f(10)$
    $10$ is in $[-10, 10]$, so use $f(x) = 2x - 5$
    $f(10) = 2(10) - 5 = 15$

  Step 3: Evaluate $f(20)$
    $20$ is in $x > 10$, so use $f(x) = 3x + 1$
    $f(20) = 3(20) + 1 = 61$

  Step 4: State the domain
    Domain: $x \geq -10$

💡 Worked Example 2 — A real-world piecewise model
A taxi charges $3 for the first 2 km and $2 per additional km. Write $C(d)$ for distance $d$ km.

  Step 1: Define the intervals
    First 2 km: flat rate
    Beyond 2 km: additional charge

  Step 2: Write the function
    $$C(d) = \begin{cases} 3 & \text{for $0 < d \leq 2$} \\ 3 + 2(d - 2) & \text{for $d > 2$} \end{cases}$$

  Step 3: Simplify the second piece
    $C(d) = 3 + 2d - 4 = 2d - 1$ for $d > 2$

  Step 4: Verify at the boundary
    At $d = 2$: first piece gives $3$
    At $d = 2$: second piece gives $2(2) - 1 = 3$  ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always check which interval the input belongs to before substituting
• Graphs of piecewise functions may have jumps at boundary points
• For continuous piecewise functions, the pieces must meet at the boundary
• The domain is the union of all individual intervals
• Piecewise models are common in economics (tax brackets), transport (fares), and physics (motion)

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the wrong formula at the boundary point. Always check whether the boundary value is included in the first interval ($\leq$ or $\geq$) or the second interval ($<$ or $>$). Also, when writing piecewise models from word problems, forgetting to subtract the initial amount from the variable — the charge for additional km is per km BEYOND the initial distance, not per total km.

notes.heading: Absolute Value Functions
notes.body:
The absolute value function returns the distance of a number from zero. It creates a characteristic V-shape and is useful for modelling tolerances, distances, and symmetric errors.

📌 Definition
For any real number $x$:

    $$|x| = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \geq 0 \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}$$

    The graph of $y = |x|$ is a V with its vertex at the origin.

🔑 Key Concept
Transformations apply to absolute value graphs in the same way as other functions:

    $$y = |x - h| + k$$

    Vertex at $(h, k)$
    $h > 0$ shifts right; $k > 0$ shifts up
    Vertical stretch by factor $a$ when $y = a|x|$

💡 Worked Example 1 — Solving $|x| = a$
Solve $|2x - 3| = 5$.

  Step 1: Split into two linear equations
    $2x - 3 = 5$  or  $2x - 3 = -5$

  Step 2: Solve each equation
    $2x = 8$  →  $x = 4$
    $2x = -2$  →  $x = -1$

  Step 3: State the solution set
    $x = 4$ or $x = -1$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Sketching $y = |f(x)|$
Sketch $y = |x^2 - 4|$.

  Step 1: Sketch $y = x^2 - 4$
    Parabola with roots at $x = \pm 2$ and vertex at $(0, -4)$

  Step 2: Reflect negative parts above the $x$-axis
    The portion below the $x$-axis ($-2 < x < 2$) is reflected upward
    New vertex at $(0, 4)$; roots remain at $x = \pm 2$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $|x| \geq 0$ always
• $|x| = a$ has two solutions when $a > 0$, one solution when $a = 0$, and no solution when $a < 0$
• $|x - h|$ measures distance from $h$ on the number line
• The modulus function is even: $|-x| = |x|$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the second case when solving $|expression| = a$. Always write both the positive and negative branch, then check that each solution is valid.

✅ Check
Solve $|x + 1| = 3$. You should get $x = 2$ or $x = -4$.

notes.heading: Exponential Functions and Asymptotes
notes.body:
Exponential functions describe rapid growth or decay. They appear in population models, compound interest, cooling curves, and radioactive decay.

📌 Definition
An exponential function has the form:

    $$f(x) = a \cdot b^x + c$$

    where $a \neq 0$, $b > 0$, $b \neq 1$
    $a$ = vertical stretch/reflection
    $b$ = base (growth if $b > 1$, decay if $0 < b < 1$)
    $c$ = vertical shift

🔑 Horizontal Asymptote
As $x \to \infty$ or $x \to -\infty$, $b^x$ approaches $0$.

    $$\text{Horizontal asymptote: } y = c$$

    The graph approaches but never touches this line.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Growth model
A population is modelled by $P(t) = 200 \cdot 1.05^t$. Find the population after 4 years.

  Step 1: Substitute $t = 4$
    $P(4) = 200 \cdot 1.05^4$

  Step 2: Calculate
    $1.05^4 \approx 1.2155$
    $P(4) \approx 200 \cdot 1.2155 = 243.1$

  Step 3: Interpret
    Population after 4 years is approximately $243$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Decay and asymptote
A medicine decays according to $M(t) = 80 \cdot 0.7^t + 5$, where $t$ is in hours. State the initial amount and long-term amount.

  Step 1: Initial amount
    $M(0) = 80 \cdot 0.7^0 + 5 = 80 + 5 = 85$ mg

  Step 2: Long-term amount
    As $t \to \infty$, $0.7^t \to 0$
    $M(t) \to 5$ mg

  Step 3: Asymptote
    Horizontal asymptote: $M = 5$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Domain of any exponential function is all real $x$
• Range depends on the vertical shift: if $a > 0$, range is $y > c$; if $a < 0$, range is $y < c$
• The $y$-intercept is found by setting $x = 0$
• Exponential growth/decay is always positive for positive bases

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing the roles of $a$ and $c$. The horizontal asymptote is $y = c$, not $y = 0$, unless $c = 0$.

flashcards.definition: Each input maps to exactly one output.
$f$ has inverse iff every horizontal line meets graph at most once.
A function defined by different expressions on different intervals.
A function that is its own inverse: $f(f(x)) = x$.
The set of $x$ in domain of $g$ such that $g(x)$ is in domain of $f$.
Applying a function and then its inverse returns the original input.

flashcards.example: $f(x) = 200 \cdot 1.05^x$ models 5% growth from an initial value of 200.

questions.explanation: For $f(x)=x^2+1$, substituting $-x$ gives $(-x)^2+1=x^2+1=f(x)$, so it is even.

questions.stem: $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=x-3$. What is the domain of $(f \circ g)(x)$?
questions.explanation: $(f \circ g)(x)=\sqrt{x-3}$. The output of $g$ must lie in the domain of $f$, so $x-3\geq 0 \to x\geq 3$.
For $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$, solving $y=\frac{1}{x}$ gives $x=\frac{1}{y}$, so $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{x}=f(x)$. Its graph is also symmetric about $y=x$.

questions.stem: A taxi charges $3 for the first 2 km and $2 per additional km. Which piecewise function gives the cost $C(d)$ in dollars for distance $d$ km?
questions.explanation: The first 2 km cost a flat $3. Beyond that, each extra kilometre adds $2, so the cost is $3+2(d-2)$.

questions.stem: $f(x)=x^2-4x+5$ is restricted to $x\leq 2$ so it has an inverse. What is $f^{-1}(x)$?
questions.explanation: Complete the square: $f(x)=(x-2)^2+1$. With $x\leq 2$, solving $y=(x-2)^2+1$ gives $x-2=-\sqrt{y-1}$, so $x=2-\sqrt{y-1}$. Hence $f^{-1}(x)=2-\sqrt{x-1}$.

questions.stem: A cup of coffee cools from $90^\circ\text{C}$ according to $T(t)=70 \times 0.9^t+20$, where $t$ is minutes. What temperature does it approach long-term?
questions.explanation: As $t\to\infty$, $0.9^t\to 0$, so $T\to 20^\circ\text{C}$. This horizontal asymptote represents the room temperature the coffee approaches but never goes below.
$2x - 1 = 7$ gives $x = 4$, and $2x - 1 = -7$ gives $x = -3$. Both values satisfy the original equation.

questions.stem: What is the horizontal asymptote of $f(x) = 50 \cdot 0.8^x + 10$?
questions.explanation: As $x \to \infty$, $0.8^x \to 0$, so $f(x) \to 10$. The horizontal asymptote is therefore $y = 10$.
The graph of $y = |x - h| + k$ has vertex $(h, k)$. Here $h = 3$ and $k = 2$, so the vertex is $(3, 2)$.
